1. Row Picture Row picture is a way to view each linear equation in a system as a geometric shape. It could be a line in 2D or a flat plane in 3D. We draw those shapes to see where they intersect.  The intersection point is the answer of our System of Equations.

MIT 18.06 · Lecture 3 Matrix Multiplication & Inverses  Based on Gilbert Strang’s lecture
Roadmap 1. Showing 4 different ways of matrices multiplication    2.Inverse matrices   3. Application
Four ways to compute C = AB Rows of and Columns of B, same answer every time. 1 · Dot products 2 · Columns 3 · Rows 4 · Columns × rows

1: dot products Example A : [1 2] B : [5; 7] C = 1·5 + 2·7 = 19 shop 2: 3·5 + 4·7 = 43 Each entry of  C = AB  is a dot product: c_ij  = (row  i  of A) · (col j of B) the number of columns in the first matrix (A) must be equal to the number of rows in the second matrix (B) A: m × n B: n × p C: m × p

2 and 3: columns and rows Each column of C is A times the matching column of B, so it is a linear combination of the columns of A.  Each row of C is the matching row of A times B, a linear combination of the rows of B. C = 5·[1;3] + 7·[2;4] = [19; 43] C = 1·[5 6] + 2·[7 8] = [19 22] Example C = 5·[1;3] + 7·[2;4] = [19; 43] C = 1·[5 6] + 2·[7 8] = [19 22]

4: columns times rows take a  row  from the first matrix and a  column  from the second matrix, multiply their corresponding numbers together, and then  add  those products up. Example A : [ 1; 2; 3] B : [1 3 ] AB =[ 1 3; 2 6; 3 9]
The inverse matrix Only exists when the matrices is a square and the determinant ≠ 0 Example A = [3 1; 4 2]
Gauss-Jordan: finding A⁻¹ Start [ A | I ] Row-reduce Eliminate up and down Finish [ I | A⁻¹ ]

Example 1. Setup A = [1 3; 2 5] Write [A | I] and row-reduce until the left side becomes I. Initial augmented matrix [ 1 3 | 1 0 ] [ 2 5 | 0 1 ] 2. Gauss-Jordan Step 1: R2 − 2·R1 [ 1 3 | 1 0 ] [ 0 -1 | -2 1 ] Step 2: R2 × (−1) [ 1 3 | 1 0 ] [ 0 1 | 2 -1 ] Step 3: R1 − 3·R2 [ 1 0 | -5 3 ] [ 0 1 | 2 -1 ] 3. Solution The right side now contains the inverse matrix A⁻¹. Inverse matrix A⁻¹ [ -5 3 ] [ 2 -1 ] Check: [1 3; 2 5]·[−5 3; 2 −1] = I
MATLAB demo: multiplication A = [1 2; 3 4]; B = [5 6; 7 8]; C = A*B C =     19    22     43    50 Expected output

MATLAB demo: multiplication A = [1 3; 2 5]; M =  rref ([A eye(2)])     % Gauss-Jordan on [A | I] Ainv  = M(:,3:4)          % right half is the inverse A* Ainv                    % check: should be the identity inv(A)                   % built-in check M =      1     0    -5     3      0     1     2    -1 Ainv  =     -5     3      2    -1

Where this is used AI Graphics Transforms 3D coordinates (rotation, scaling and projection) by multiplying vectors (points in space) with transformation matrices Cybersecurity Hill cipher: ciphertext = K·message. Decrypting needs K⁻¹, so a singular key cannot decrypt. Layers in neural networks multiply input feature vectors by massive weight matrices followed by non-linear activations.
